extracted.intended_audience: students and self-learners aiming to think like mathematicians (undergraduate proof students and general math learners)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for students and self-learners on developing deep, conceptual understanding of mathematics (especially proofs) rather than rote computation; guidance on study habits, explanation, and perspective-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grapple with the mathematics (work hard to understand every aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To fully understand a piece of mathematics, you have to grapple with it. You have to work hard to fully understand every aspect of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the subject from all angles (author's phone analogy): know where each part is, open it up to see inner workings, and study it—really study it—to develop a deep understanding. Active struggle and close examination are required; avoid superficial reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid robot/rote learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat math as mere symbol-manipulation or speedy arithmetic computations; avoid being a 'robot' who only follows instructions without understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize 'robot-symptoms' (memorizing formulas, mechanically performing computations) and shift toward questioning what you are doing and why. The post contrasts being a robot with being someone who has ideas and can think critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize conceptual clarity over speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding things clearly is more important than speed or computational fluency: 'learning how to learn doesn't necessarily mean you'll learn faster.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that deep understanding takes time; aim to 'see things clearly' even if you remain slow at symbol-pushing or mental arithmetic. Long-term clarity and insight are the goals rather than quick answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek unifying/foundational ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask 'what is it that they all have in common?' to find underlying principles that unify seemingly different phenomena (author cites affinity for category theory as an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unifying perspectives to determine when different phenomena are governed by the same underlying principles; this helps form deeper insight and guides further study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice explaining and writing mathematics well
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding the right words to share mathematics is important; strive to both 'understand things clearly and explain them well' (quote from Chris Olah).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distillation process for clear exposition is lengthy—expect to iterate on explanations. Developing good notation/phrasing and pedagogical clarity is part of learning and teaching mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be patient and persistent (learning takes time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep learning and the ability to explain mathematics require sustained effort and time; projects like writing and thesis work slow other activities like blogging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat development of understanding and communication as long-term processes. Don't measure progress solely by short-term output frequency; accept slower, deliberate practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn proof fundamentals through active engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides meta-skills, learn basic proof techniques and logical foundations (the author mentions truth tables and proof by contradiction as examples encountered in an intro-to-proofs class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine learning concrete proof tools with the broader habit of grappling; use introductory formal techniques as building blocks for conceptual understanding rather than rote procedures.
